The commercial opens in a stylized nighttime landscape under a deep blue sky with dark clouds and a low line of mountains on the horizon. Across a wide, misty plain stand countless pale rectangular refrigerators, arranged like rows of upright monuments stretching far into the distance. Some are close enough to show simple door divisions, while many more appear as small white blocks fading into the haze. The scene has a cool, blue, almost dreamlike look, with fog drifting low around the appliances. As the view moves through this field, larger refrigerators pass in the foreground, their beige or off-white surfaces briefly filling the sides of the image. One tall appliance slides very close on the right, revealing dark vertical handles before it passes out of view. The mass of older-looking refrigerators remains behind it, still spread across the misty ground beneath the dark sky. A single new refrigerator then stands alone on the open plain, centered against the mountain horizon. It is a tall, light-colored side-by-side model with two full-length doors and dark vertical handles. The doors begin to open outward. First a narrow strip of bright interior light appears, then both doors swing wider to reveal a fully stocked refrigerator and freezer. The inside is brightly lit and organized with shelves, bins, and door compartments holding bottles, cartons, jars, packaged foods, and other groceries. The left side has narrower compartments, while the right side has wider shelves and storage racks. The open doors frame the food display, making the refrigerator the only bright, detailed object in the otherwise dark blue landscape. The scene shifts to a modern-looking Maytag dealer building set in the same nighttime environment. The building is low, angular, and white, with strong blue lighting outlining its edges and open showroom windows. A Maytag sign is visible near the roofline. Inside the lit showroom, appliances and counters can be seen, along with several people. Figures in dark clothing stand or walk near the entrance and counter; one person appears beside another near the front, while other people are visible behind the counter area. Small white disclaimer text appears along the bottom of the screen: “Limited to sealed refrigeration system and original purchase price. Limited time offer.” The dealership remains in view as the people continue standing and moving in small groups near the entrance and showroom counter. The blue glow around the building contrasts with the dark sky and mountain silhouettes behind it, making the store look like a bright island in the open landscape. The commercial returns to the refrigerator standing alone on the misty plain. Its doors are open again, and the interior shelves remain brightly lit and packed with groceries. The final view shows the refrigerator turned slightly at an angle, emphasizing its side-by-side design and the dark ice-and-water dispenser area on the left door. Large white capital letters appear across the bottom: “GUARANTEED UNTIL 2000 A.D.” The refrigerator remains upright and prominent against the dark blue sky and distant mountains.

A black audio cassette rests inside a clear plastic cassette case on a plain grey surface. The cassette label includes “SONY” and “UCX-S 90.” A hand enters from the left, steadies the case, and opens the transparent lid. The cassette is slid downward and lifted out, leaving the hinged plastic case empty and open, with its two small internal pegs visible against the grey background. The empty case remains centered. Instead of simply staying empty, it begins to be filled with electronics. A hand places a pale green circuit board into the upper right portion of the case, its tiny black chips, silver contacts, and printed pathways visible. A smaller green circuit board is set into the lower left. Another compact mechanical part is brought in by both hands and fitted over the boards; it has small metal brackets and dark components, like the inner workings of a tape player. The hands press the pieces into place carefully, as if assembling a miniature device inside the cassette case. The view shifts closer to a silver metal mechanism with two large circular reel areas and small black spindles. A hand slides another small green circuit board into the side of this metal plate. The parts line up tightly, emphasizing how compact the assembly is. The partly built device then appears inside a rectangular silver housing. The word “STEREO” is printed near the top right, and small control buttons or knobs sit along the upper edge. The original black cassette, still marked “UCX-S 90,” lies above the device on the grey surface, acting as a size comparison. Hands now add the front portion of the player. A silver faceplate with two round reel-window shapes is guided into place over the exposed mechanism. The fingers adjust it on both sides, pressing it down so the two circular areas align. A dark smoked plastic cover is then lifted from below and swung up across the front. As it closes, the finished unit is revealed: a compact silver Sony Walkman with a black oval window showing the two circular reel shapes beneath. Across the top front, “SONY” appears on the left and “WALKMAN” in red on the right, with a thin red line near the top edge. The assembled player sits neatly on the grey surface, with the cassette still lying above it. A white earphone cord is draped across the Walkman, looping diagonally over the front window and across the brand name area. Large white on-screen lettering fades in over the product: “SONY,” with the smaller slogan beneath it, “THE ONE AND ONLY.” The Walkman remains visible behind the bold text, partly covered by the crossing earphone cord. The final scene shows a freestanding in-store display on a dark surface. It is a tall white sign held upright by dark side supports, with a picture of the Walkman near the lower middle and a pair of white earphones lying in front to the left. Large blue text at the top reads: “Listen to the new Sony Super Walkman. You might win to the tune of $25,000.” Small fine print appears along the bottom of the screen, including “No Purchase Necessary,” entry-card information, and an offer expiration date, though some of the smaller wording is difficult to read.

A living room appears with warm, dim lighting and a slightly soft 1980s video look. A man, seen mostly from behind, stands beside a wooden chair and a small television set on a table. He wears a light short-sleeved shirt and light trousers. A potted plant hangs or stands to the left, and a tall lamp with a pale shade is on the right. The room has a lived-in domestic feel, with a chair, side table, and small objects around the seating area. The television is then shown more closely: an older box-style set with a rounded screen and control knobs on the right side, sitting on a wooden table with framed photos and small decorative items on top. The screen looks pale and inactive or filled with blank static. A close view of the floor lamp follows. Its cream-colored shade glows warmly at first, then the light visibly fades until the shade is dark, demonstrating an appliance being turned off. The product package is then displayed upright on a tabletop. The box reads “The Clapper” in large yellow letters, with the phrases “Clap it on!” and “Clap it off!” printed around the name. On the front are pictures of hands clapping and small demonstration images of a television and a hand near a device. The box also says “Sound activated on/off switch for appliances.” The package is shown progressively closer so the branding and instructions dominate the view. A woman stands inside a home entryway in front of a light-colored front door with narrow glass panels on both sides. She appears to be an adult woman with dark hair, wearing a light coat and dark pants. She stands on a small rug, facing into the house, with her arms held forward as if she has just clapped or is demonstrating clapping from the doorway. The surrounding hallway is dimmer, with a staircase visible to one side. The setup of the device is then shown in close-up. A black wall outlet is mounted on vertical wood paneling. A hand brings a white rectangular device toward the outlet. The device has a ribbed front, a small dark sensor-like dot near the upper area, and a thicker, plug-in body. The hand presses it into the outlet until it sits flat against the wall. Once installed, the white Clapper unit covers the black outlet plate; two small rectangular controls or plug areas are visible near the bottom of the front. An elderly woman with short, fluffy white hair appears against a plain light background. She wears a patterned cardigan with colorful zigzag stripes over a white blouse with a dark bow at the neck, and small earrings. She smiles gently, looking pleased, then lowers her gaze and closes her eyes slightly as if concentrating on or completing the demonstration, likely clapping with her hands below the edge of the picture. The plugged-in Clapper unit is shown again on the wood-paneled wall, emphasizing the installed product. The elderly woman is then seen lying in bed, propped on pillows beneath a wooden headboard. She is covered by white bedding and smiles comfortably. A wider view reveals the bedroom: she lies on the right side of the bed, a lit lamp stands nearby, and a small television sits to the left with a blue-toned screen. Curtains with a patterned fabric hang behind the bed area, and the room looks cozy and softly lit. The arrangement shows the device being useful from bed, with the lamp and television within the room but not within easy reach. The commercial ends on a black background with a product box image and large white “The Clapper” logo, again accompanied by the words “Clap it on” and “Clap it off.” Store logos appear below and around it. Visible names include Woolworth, Perry Drug Stores, Snyder, Red Owl, and Elliott’s Ace Hardware, with a Walgreens-style logo also shown.

The commercial opens in a bright, busy office made up of gray cubicles, desks, filing cabinets, framed prints, plants, and large windows along the far wall. Several office workers move in the background. In one cubicle, a woman with short dark hair, wearing a pale sweater and a patterned scarf, sits at a desk covered with papers, a pencil cup, an open book, and a computer. She raises one arm high above the cubicle wall as if signaling to someone nearby. As the scene shifts across the partitions, a young man in a striped dress shirt and dark tie is visible in a neighboring cubicle, seated at a cluttered desk with papers, an open book, and photographs pinned to the wall. He reaches upward toward the top of the partition. A hand lifts a small electronic device above the cubicle wall. It is a compact gray-and-black rectangle, about the size of a large calculator, with a narrow display screen at the top, a miniature keyboard below, and a column of rounded buttons on the right side. The man sits below with one arm still stretched up, looking toward the device, while his desk remains piled with work materials. He appears to be involved in passing or reclaiming the device across the office partition. Back at the woman’s desk, she holds the device in both hands and smiles down at it. Her cubicle has a computer monitor to her left, a desk lamp, a pencil holder, an open notebook, and personal items on the walls, including a small stuffed animal or toy figure and pinned pictures. She looks comfortable and amused as she uses the device. A close view of the product shows the label “Spell-Checker” above the display. The screen first reads “READY...” while a pencil tip points near the display and keys. Small white on-screen text at the bottom reads “BATTERIES NOT INCLUDED.” Fingers press the tiny black letter keys, and the display shows an entered approximation of a word, beginning with letters like “AQ” and then “AQUIR,” suggesting a phonetic or misspelled entry. The device then shows “SEARCHING.” Another view shows the full unit in a hand, with the Texas Instruments logo and name printed on the right side. A thumb presses one of the side buttons, illustrating the special function keys. The display then shows spelling results such as “ACQUIRABLE” and later “ACQUIRED,” with small indicator text beneath the word. The young man reappears, leaning around the edge of a cubicle partition into the aisle. He has dark, full hair, a striped shirt, and a loose dark tie, and he looks toward the woman with a playful, expectant expression. The woman turns toward him while holding the spell checker close to her chest, smiling. He steps into her cubicle area and stands beside her desk, leaning forward with one hand on the desktop and gesturing with the other. She remains seated, still holding the device, and looks down at it as if checking another word while he watches closely over her shoulder. The device is then placed on a light wood desktop beside an open notebook with handwritten lines. A small glass paperweight sits nearby. The Texas Instruments Spell-Checker rests flat on the desk, its screen and keyboard clearly visible, with the “Spell-Checker” label on the left and “Texas Instruments” branding on the right. A hand adjusts it, then withdraws, leaving the product centered as the focus of the scene. Another hand reaches in from the left as if about to take it. At the end, the woman and the young man are together at her desk. She is seated, smiling broadly, while he leans over the desktop with both hands down, grinning. The spell checker lies between them near the notebook and paperweight, presented as the object they have been sharing and using.

A black Sony audio cassette rests inside a clear plastic cassette case on a plain grey surface. Its front label has a long white strip and small printed markings, including the Sony name and the model marking “UCX-S90.” A pair of light-skinned hands moves in from the sides, grips the case, flips it open, and slides the cassette out. The transparent lid remains open, exposing the empty case with its molded plastic posts and shallow compartments. With the cassette removed, the open clear case stays centered, now looking like an empty rectangular shell. Small electronic parts begin to appear inside it. A hand lowers in a green circuit board shaped to fit along the upper and right edges of the case, covered with tiny silver components, black chips, and soldered details. Another smaller green board is placed near the lower left. Then a compact grey mechanical assembly is set into the middle, with small metal parts and a dark circular wheel, suggesting the inner workings of a cassette player being built where the cassette used to be. The view shifts closer to more mechanical pieces: pale metal plates, circular reel areas, dark hubs, screws, and a green circuit strip. Hands guide these parts into place, sliding a small circuit board into the side of the metal cassette mechanism. Two round silver reel-like discs settle into a flat rectangular metal body, each with a black central spindle. The parts look precise and miniature, filling a space about the size of the original cassette case. The assembled mechanism is now shown inside a compact rectangular player. The top portion has tiny controls and a label reading “STEREO.” A separate Sony cassette remains lying above it in the background as a size comparison. The hands bring a front cover down over the exposed workings. As the cover closes, the device becomes a finished silver Sony Walkman. Across the top front, the text “SONY” appears on the left and “WALKMAN” in red on the right. A wide rounded rectangular window spans the lower front, through which the two circular reel shapes are visible. Small buttons line the top edge. The finished Walkman sits alone on the grey surface, neat and compact, with the cassette still above it. A white earphone cord is placed across the front, looping diagonally over the Walkman and trailing off to the side. Large white title text fades over the product: “SONY” in huge capital letters, with “THE ONE AND ONLY” below it. The Walkman remains visible behind the translucent lettering, partly crossed by the white cord. The final image changes to a store display card standing upright on a dark surface, with a pair of white earphones lying to its left. The display shows a picture of the Walkman in a dark square near the lower half. Large blue text at the top reads, “Listen to the new Sony Super Walkman. You might win to the tune of $25,000.” At the very bottom, small white legal text appears, including “No Purchase Necessary,” “Entry Cards Available at Participating Retailers,” and an offer expiration date in November 1983, followed by the usual restriction that the offer is void where prohibited by law.

A chilled green glass beer bottle stands on the left beside a tall, narrow beer glass on the right. Both are set on a dark tabletop against a softly lit grey background. The bottle is covered with beads of condensation, and at first its front label is turned mostly away, so the bottle appears as a glossy green shape with only a dark, partial label area visible. The glass is filled with golden amber beer and topped with a thick, smooth white foam head that rises slightly above the rim. The beer glows warmly, with bubbles and highlights visible through the glass. The bottle and filled glass remain side by side, evenly spaced, like a simple studio product display. The amber beer stays steady in the glass, and the foam cap remains rounded and dense. A hand enters from above and grips the neck of the bottle with thumb and fingers. The hand begins to rotate the bottle, turning it so that the label faces forward. As it turns, more of the white and green label comes into view. The bottle is now presented front-on. Its oval label is clearly visible, with the Heineken name across the center and surrounding label text including “Imported Beer.” The green bottle still looks cold and wet with condensation. A smaller neck label is also visible near the top. The glass of beer remains to the right, upright on its stem, with the bright golden liquid and white foam head forming a clean contrast against the darker background. Near the end, another hand reaches in from the right and wraps around the stem of the beer glass. The hand lifts the glass slightly from the tabletop while the Heineken bottle remains standing to the left with its label facing forward. The final image holds the bottle and the lifted glass together, emphasizing the chilled bottle, the branded label, and the freshly poured beer.

A close view of a white electric stovetop shows a hand pressing a tan rectangular piece, like a block of sandpaper, flat against the enamel surface. Black coil burners sit to either side, and chrome control knobs are visible along the back edge. The hand rubs the tan block back and forth over the stovetop, suggesting an exaggerated, harsh way to clean it. The view widens to a home kitchen. A middle-aged man with light skin, short dark hair, and a beige button-down shirt stands at the stove. A large brass- or copper-colored pot sits on the right side of the stovetop. The man holds the tan cleaning block in one hand and looks down at the stove, then toward the viewer, as if presenting the example. The kitchen behind him has dark wood cabinets, a built-in oven, a sink area, and bright daylight coming from a window. A teal cylindrical can labeled in large white letters “SCOURING POWDER” stands upright on the stovetop between the black coil burners. A crumpled white cloth or paper towel lies beside it. The can is presented alone in the center of the stove surface, making it the focus. The man appears again from the chest up in the kitchen, facing forward. He then raises a white plastic bottle with a dark oval label and yellow lettering reading “Soft Scrub,” holding it near his shoulder so the label faces outward. The demonstration moves back to the stovetop. Small white text at the top reads “USE ONLY AS DIRECTED.” The white stove surface around one burner is smeared with yellowish-brown spills and stains. The copper-colored pot remains on the left. The man holds a lavender rectangular sponge in one hand and the Soft Scrub bottle in the other. He tilts the bottle downward and squeezes a line of thick white cleanser onto the sponge. He sets the bottle upright nearby with the Soft Scrub label still visible, then presses the lavender sponge onto the stained white enamel. With his other hand he scrubs in short strokes around the burner area, moving the sponge across the brownish spill marks. The white cleanser spreads into a pale film as he works. The pot stays at the left edge of the stove, its side marked with cooking stains, while the black coil burner sits just behind the cleaning area. The scrubbing continues across the front-right area of the stovetop. The sponge moves back and forth, then side to side, covering the stained patch. The Soft Scrub bottle stands in the background to the right, label facing forward, while the man’s hand keeps the sponge flat against the surface. As he wipes, the area looks cleaner and whiter, with fewer visible stains. He lifts the sponge slightly and moves it toward the pot, then sets it aside near the pot handle. With his free hand, he rubs a fingertip across the cleaned white surface, tracing along the edge of the wiped area as if checking for leftover grit or residue. The man returns in a medium view, facing the viewer in the kitchen. He holds up a small pinch or speck between his fingers near his face, using the gesture to illustrate what has been removed or what is not left behind. The final product display returns to the stovetop. The teal “SCOURING POWDER” can stands on the left, with the pot on the right in the background. Large white on-screen text appears over the stove: “Cleans like a scouring powder, but doesn’t scratch like one.” A hand slides the white Soft Scrub bottle into the foreground, placing it in front of the scouring powder can. The bottle remains standing on the left side of the screen, label facing forward, while the slogan fills the right side over the stovetop.

The commercial opens in a stark black-and-white studio space. A casually dressed adult man with medium-length dark hair and facial hair sits facing forward in a large cushioned armchair placed on a round braided rug. He wears a plaid robe or loose shirt, light pants, and sneakers, with his feet stretched out in front of him and his hands resting on the chair arms. The background is otherwise empty and bright. A small black television set appears alone against the same white background. Its screen first shows static, then changes to a Soloflex image: the bold word “SOLOFLEX” above a simple drawing of the exercise machine. A thick hand-drawn black arrow points toward the TV from the left. The toll-free number “1-800-762-FREE” appears in large white lettering on a black rectangular bar across the TV screen, then the TV fades away so the number remains by itself on the white background, with another black arrow pointing down toward it. The scene changes to a close-up of a smiling female-presenting telephone operator in a headset, shown in a vintage switchboard setting. She has styled dark hair, wears jewelry including rings, and holds one hand near her ear while the headset microphone curves toward her mouth. Beside her, rows of switchboard plugs and jacks fill the right side of the image. She looks engaged and pleasant, as if taking the call. On the white background, printed Soloflex materials are displayed: a brochure or manual with a drawing of a muscular torso, and a dark videocassette or video case with a photograph of a muscular chest and the word “SOLOFLEX” at the top. A black arrow points up toward these materials. The toll-free number “1-800-762-FREE” appears again by itself, this time with an arrow pointing in from the right. A delivery worker in a cap and uniform pushes a very large cardboard shipping box on a hand truck. The box is tilted diagonally and nearly as tall as the worker. It is printed with “SOLOFLEX” and shipping markings including “THIS SIDE UP,” “LAY FLAT,” and “DO NOT PLACE ON END.” The worker grips the hand truck handle and smiles toward the viewer as the oversized package dominates the scene. The Soloflex machine itself is then shown assembled on the white studio floor. It has a vertical upright post, a curved support frame, a flat padded bench, a horizontal bar, and a base labeled “SOLOFLEX.” The design is compact and minimal, with dark metal parts standing out against the pale background. The phone number reappears once more, centered on a black bar with an arrow pointing toward it. A shirtless, athletic adult man in light shorts begins demonstrating exercises on the machine. In a close view, he stands beside the vertical post and grips a horizontal bar with both hands at hip level, performing a curl-like movement as the bar rises toward his waist. A drawn arrow points toward the machine’s upright column. His posture is controlled, and his gaze is directed downward toward the bar. The exercise sequence continues with the same man lying on an angled bench, knees bent and feet braced against the machine. With his hands near his head, he curls his upper body upward in a sit-up or abdominal crunch. The machine’s curved frame and upright post are visible to the side, and a black arrow points toward his bent legs and the movement area. He then appears front-facing with a padded bar across the back of his shoulders, squatting on the machine platform. His knees are bent, feet planted, and he rises through the squat with a focused expression. A high-contrast silhouette follows: the man’s body is shown in black profile against a white background, with his legs bent and supported near the machine’s upright post. He curls his torso upward toward his knees, emphasizing an abdominal movement. The vertical post with a line of adjustment holes appears at the left, and a drawn arrow points down toward his torso and knees. The silhouette makes the body position and movement stand out clearly. In a low, close view from beside the bench, the shirtless man lies on his back and grips a bar above his chest for a press. His hands hold the bar wide apart; his arms bend and extend as the bar moves over his chest and toward his face. The machine’s metal frame surrounds him, and a black arrow points toward his chest and the pressing motion. His muscles are highlighted by the black-and-white lighting. Another silhouette exercise is shown in profile. The man holds a handle or bar close to his chin with one fist while a long resistance arm angles back toward the machine on the right. He leans back and lowers his upper body, then pulls against the resistance, the fist staying near his face as the arm and shoulder engage. A black arrow points from the right toward the working position. The phone number “1-800-762-FREE” returns again on the plain white background, with an arrow pointing up toward it. A round wall clock appears, black-rimmed with large numbers and hands clustered around 12, suggesting a short amount of time. A hand-drawn arrow points toward the clock. The visual shifts to a flipping desk calendar. A page marked “MONDAY 13” is visible in bold type, surrounded by blurred duplicate calendar pages as if time is passing quickly. A hand turns the page, and the calendar changes to “WEDNESDAY 15.” The Wednesday page remains centered for several moments, then another hand turn reveals “FRIDAY 17.” The pages are large, with bold black numbers and weekday names on white paper, held on metal rings at the top. The phone number appears again with an arrow pointing down to it. A shaggy, light-colored dog sits alone on the white background, facing forward with an alert, friendly expression. Its mouth is slightly open, and its ears hang down. A black arrow points toward the dog’s head, visually matching the spoken reference to how the dog looks. A close-up of a shirtless torso and loose jeans follows. The waist of the jeans appears too large, with extra space around the abdomen. A hand pulls a belt strap across the front, showing multiple belt holes as it tightens the pants. A black arrow points toward the slimmer waist area and the looseness of the jeans. The phone number returns again, centered on the white background with an arrow pointing upward at it. The athletic man reappears from the chest up, shirtless and sweaty, facing forward. At first the phone number briefly overlays his chest, then disappears. He throws his head back with his mouth wide open, fists clenched near his sides and chest, as if exulting after a workout. His hair is damp and pushed back, his eyes close or squint with effort, and sweat glistens down the center of his chest. He continues pumping his arms and holding the triumphant open-mouthed expression while a black arrow at the left points toward him. The phone number “1-800-762-FREE” appears once more on a black rectangular bar with a downward arrow above it. The final product image returns: the Soloflex machine stands alone on the white background, with the large bold word “SOLOFLEX” above it and the base also labeled “SOLOFLEX.” The commercial ends on the phone number again, now surrounded by many hand-drawn black arrows from every direction, all pointing inward toward “1-800-762-FREE.”

A bronze or gold Oldsmobile sedan is displayed in a clean side profile, facing to the right, against a warm amber-brown studio background with a smoky, softly glowing atmosphere. The car has four doors, a long low body, dark-tinted windows, and polished wheels, with its silhouette emphasized by dramatic lighting from above and behind. The floor beneath it is dark and reflective, giving the car a showroom-like presentation. No people are visible. Across the bottom of the image, large white serif text identifies the vehicle: “Oldsmobile Eighty Eight LSS.”

A plain white refrigerator stands alone in the center of a sparse studio-like room. The floor is a gray-and-white checkerboard pattern, and the background is a smooth pale gray wall with soft light centered behind the appliance. The refrigerator has a top freezer section, a larger lower door, a vertical handle on the right, and a small brand badge near the upper right of the freezer door. The view moves in close to the refrigerator’s upper edge. From behind the white appliance surface, the top of a man’s head rises into view. He is a large Black man with close-cropped dark hair and a mustache, wearing an all-white athletic outfit. As more of him appears, he leans over the refrigerator edge with both arms forward. His right wrist is wrapped in a thick white athletic wristband, and a ring is visible on one hand. He looks down with a focused, slightly amused expression while moving his hands along the white surface in front of him, as if working on or cleaning part of the refrigerator just below the visible edge. He then lowers his head and shoulders back down until only the top of his hair is visible, and then disappears. The refrigerator is again seen standing by itself in the same empty room. A moment later, the man peeks out from behind the right side of the appliance. Only part of his face and shoulder are visible at first, pressed close to the refrigerator’s side. He smiles broadly, looking toward the open space to his right, then ducks back behind it. The full room comes back into view. The refrigerator remains centered, and the man emerges from behind its right side. He is dressed entirely in white football-style gear: a loose white jersey, white football pants, white socks, white high-top athletic shoes, and white wristbands. His build is very large and powerful. He steps beside the refrigerator, smiling, then places his hands on the side and handle area. He grips the refrigerator and begins to tip it toward himself. The appliance leans diagonally, its bottom edge lifting off the floor on one side. He braces it against his body, arms wrapped around the side, and hoists it up with apparent ease. Still smiling, he walks left across the checkerboard floor while carrying the full-size refrigerator at a slant in front of him. The refrigerator’s bottom hovers above the floor as he continues stepping sideways and forward, his white shoes crossing the patterned tiles. As he carries the refrigerator off toward the left edge of the room, large dark lettering fades in on the wall behind him. The CP&L logo appears, followed by the slogan “Where Listening Generates Powerful Ideas,” and beneath it the phone number “1-800-THE-FRIDGE.” The man and refrigerator continue moving partly out of view on the left, leaving the CP&L message and phone number clearly centered against the pale wall.

Against a plain black studio background, a white chicken fills the center of the image, its wings thrown wide and blurred from rapid flapping. Its feathers are ruffled and spread out as it drops downward toward a small dark portable CD player beneath it. The player sits alone on the black surface, with a rounded rectangular shape, a small display area on the front edge, and control buttons along the sides. The chicken continues descending, body tilted forward and head pointed down, its orange beak and pale feathers visible amid the motion blur. As it lands, its wings beat hard on either side, creating a messy, feathery cloud around its body. The bird’s orange feet come down onto the top of the CD player, using it like a tiny platform. The Magnavox name is faintly visible on the player as the chicken’s feet and body partially cover it. The bird steadies itself while still flapping. Its wings stretch out horizontally, then begin folding in. The chicken crouches low over the player, head down, feathers puffed into a rounded mound. Its orange feet grip the top surface, toes splayed across the device near the front controls. The dark background keeps all attention on the white bird and the small electronic player beneath it. Gradually, the chicken settles. Its wings tuck closer to its sides, and it stands more upright on the portable CD player. The bird lifts its head slightly and turns to one side, looking off to the right, while remaining balanced on the device. The visual joke is that the player remains in place under the significant jolt of the chicken’s landing. The commercial then changes to a clean white promotional screen. Large black text reads “Free” at the top, with a thin red line beneath it, followed by “CD Case.” Below the words is a picture of a small black zippered CD carrying case with a wrist strap. Under the case, smaller text reads, “Up to a $20 value,” followed by fine print: “Offer ends March 31, 1996. While supplies last.”

The commercial opens on an old-style computer monitor in a dark setting. Its blue screen carries a centered warning label that reads “System Error 86,” printed like a strip of paper across the display. On the wall, dark circular panels and recessed rings echo the shape of the lamp. One fixture resembles a black cone projecting straight out from a round opening. On a busy city sidewalk outside a modern glass-fronted building, a young woman with shoulder-length brown hair stands at an outdoor flower stall. A bold black word, “Triactin,” appears alone on a plain gray background, then grows soft and oversized as it fades away. As the hand continues, the circle and marks are partly erased, leaving the nervous-system lines more open and less cluttered. A Triactin liquid bottle fades in over the center of the nerve diagram, then becomes the main object on a plain tabletop. The bottle stands upright, label facing forward with the triple-action emblem and “TRIACTIN” name visible. A hand lowers a spoon in front of the bottle; the spoon has a long handle and a rounded bowl, suggesting the liquid form is measured by spoon. The tablet pack is held beside the open box, with the printed carton text still partly visible: “chewable tablets” and the same numbered list for acid stomach, digestive tension, and nervous stomach. The final product display returns to the liquid bottle on the left and the chewable-tablet box on the right, both neatly arranged on the tabletop against the gray background. The words “Calms Stomach Spasms” appear again in white lettering above the box area. The image settles on the two Triactin forms together: the upright liquid bottle and the horizontal box of chewable tablets, both clearly branded with the triple-action symbol.

Then the product arrangement returns: the Yuban can and the filled cup sit again among loose beans. A hand enters from the right, grasping the handle of the white cup. Hands scoop up beans from the sack and let them fall back in a small stream. Large white on-screen text appears over the sack reading “green beans.” The hands continue stirring and lifting the beans, emphasizing their small, pale, raw-looking appearance in the black-and-white image. The coarse weave of the burlap sack frames the mound. The comparison widens into two side-by-side bean displays. On the left, a hand holds a scoop or cloth full of darker beans, labeled with large white text “aged beans.” On the right, another hand holds a lighter-looking handful labeled “green beans.” The two labels sit near the bottom of the screen, each aligned with its respective sample. Small pale bubbles or highlights float on the coffee’s surface. A hand steadies the cup and saucer near the rim and edge, presenting the drink close to the viewer. The cup remains in close-up, full of dark coffee with a few light bubbles on top. Fingers hover and adjust around the cup and saucer, then the cup is lifted. The background becomes darker and softer, and the cup moves toward a person in formal clothing. A light-skinned adult man appears, clean-shaven, with neatly combed dark hair. He wears a dark suit jacket, a light dress shirt, and a tie. He holds the white cup by its handle at chest level, looking down toward it. His expression is restrained and thoughtful. A woman seated at a desk reaches out with a stack of papers toward him, and another person walks by with documents. A tall stack of papers sits on the desk between her and the boss. The boss now relaxes in a chair to the right, leaning back with his legs crossed and holding a small paper in his hands. His posture is calm and satisfied compared with his earlier rush. A closer view focuses on the secretary at the typewriter. She sits upright, smiling slightly, with one hand poised above the keys and the paper rising from the machine, suggesting she is preparing or sending a written reply. The final image is a clean Western Union Telegram form filling the screen. At the top, large printed text reads “WESTERN UNION” with “TELEGRAM” beneath it. In the center, inside a bold oval, handwritten-style words say, “it’s wise to wire.”

In black-and-white animation, three elaborately dressed women stand in a doorway inside a plain domestic room. They have exaggerated cartoon faces and smug smiles. One is tall and thin in a dark, formal-looking dress with puffed sleeves and a decorative headpiece; another is short and round in a patterned, ruffled skirt; the third is taller and broader, wearing a dark bodice and a light striped skirt. They cluster together, laughing and pointing toward the right, as if mocking someone out of sight. The scene shifts to the person they are pointing at: a young woman presented as Cinderella. She has long dark hair tied back with a headband and bow, a worn dark dress with ragged sleeves, and a white apron tied behind her. She bends over a large rectangular sink, scrubbing the inside with a cloth. The sink is drawn as grimy and shaded, with wavy lines rising from it to suggest dirt or fumes. A small arched window hangs on the wall behind her. Cinderella looks tired and worried, with drooping eyelids and a downturned mouth, leaning heavily over the basin as she rubs the same dirty surface again and again. A closer view emphasizes her anxious face: wide eyes, arched worried brows, and a small open mouth. She keeps scrubbing the sink, but the stains remain. As she continues, her exhausted face briefly changes into a doglike cartoon face with long floppy ears and a drooping muzzle, a visual joke showing how hard she is working. She still leans over the basin, one hand braced on the sink and the other pushing the cloth across the dirty surface. Inside a cutaway view of the sink, a small impish character appears in the dark grime. He has pointy ears, a little cap, dark clothing, and a mischievous grin. He holds a rectangular sign with large block letters reading “I’M SINK SMOG.” He laughs and lounges in the dirty basin as if he owns it. Lines and circular bubbles sweep across the sink as Cinderella’s scrubbing passes over him, but he remains in the murky bottom, knocked around but not removed. The sign tips and falls partly into the grime. Cinderella stops scrubbing and raises both hands in frustration beside the sink. She then covers her face with both hands, crying or despairing. The dirty sink is still in front of her, with the cloth draped over the edge. Over this sad image, a fantasy-like image fades in: a horse-drawn carriage rolls across a simple open background. A black horse pulls a small carriage with large wheels. A driver sits high in front, and the three formally dressed women ride in the carriage, smiling and waving as though on their way to a grand event. Cinderella is left behind at the sink. A sparkling can of Bab-O appears by itself against a plain background. The cylindrical can has large white lettering reading “BAB-O” across the top front, with a small illustrated figure on the label and a small oval callout that is too small to read clearly. Starbursts flash around the can, making it look bright and magical. The can is animated with thin little legs, as if it is walking or dancing. The sparkling Bab-O can appears near Cinderella at the sink. She now looks cleaner and more hopeful, holding both hands up in surprise as the can dissolves into a cloud of glittering stars. From the sparkles, a tiny fairy queen appears on the left. She has light hair, a small crown, wings, a full gown, and a wand tipped with a bright dot. Cinderella stands to the right of the sink, smiling with wide eyes and raised hands, watching the fairy. The fairy lifts her wand and sprinkles a shower of sparkles above the sink. Cinderella then holds a can of Bab-O out in one hand, smiling. A close view shows the can resting on an open palm. The “BAB-O” name is large and clear on the label, and sparkles glint around the top. The top of the can has shaker holes. A hand tilts the can sideways, and a stream of white powder pours out through the perforated top. The action returns to the inside of the sink, where the sink-smog imp stands in the dark basin. Bright white particles rain down over him. He looks startled as the cleaner falls around him. Soon white suds begin to form. A large hand or sweeping cleaning motion passes across the top of the basin, spreading foamy suds along the rim and down the sides. The foam grows thicker and whiter, surrounding the imp and pushing the dark grime back. The little smog character tumbles and flails inside the suds, partly buried by bubbles. The white foam swells until it fills the sink cutaway, and the dark smog shape is swallowed up. In closer views of the sink interior, mounds of bubbles fill the basin; the imp pops up in alarm, mouth open and arms raised, then is covered again and disappears among the foam. Back outside the sink, Cinderella leans over the now bright, clean basin with her hands clasped under her chin, smiling in delight. A Bab-O can stands on the counter to the left of the sink. The faucet and handles are visible at the front edge, and the sink looks clean and light instead of dark and smoky. Cinderella raises both arms joyfully, beaming. Her drab clothing transforms into a formal ball gown. The image changes to a ballroom-like scene with a checkered floor and small dancing couples in the background. Cinderella, now dressed in a strapless, full-skirted gown with a small crown or bow in her hair, holds out the side of her skirt gracefully. A prince-like man stands to her left, bowing toward her. He wears a dark formal outfit with a cape or fur-trimmed mantle and has light hair styled in a curled, royal-looking way. Cinderella smiles and shows him the clean, white result at her feet. Then she holds a can of Bab-O high in one hand while the prince bends and kisses her other hand. The commercial ends with a product display. A large Bab-O can stands in the background, with “BAB-O” clearly printed across it. In front of it, enormous white letters spelling “BAB-O” become characters with thin cartoon legs. The letters dance and march in place across the foreground, sometimes overlapping the can behind them. Finally, the letters drop lower, leaving the can centered, and bold white text appears above it: “NO SINK SMOG” on the top line and “with” beneath it. The Bab-O can remains below the words, forming the final message: “NO SINK SMOG with BAB-O.”

Cable-car tracks run down the center of the road, and the Golden Gate Bridge is visible in the hazy distance. A red-and-wood cable car sits partway up the hill, framed by the buildings and trees. Inside the open cable car, passengers sit on wooden benches beneath polished vertical poles. A uniformed male-presenting conductor in a black cap and vest stands near the front with a handheld microphone. Among the passengers are a young adult woman with long brown hair, wearing an olive-green jacket over a cream turtleneck and wide blue jeans, and a very muscular Black man with braided hair, a sleeveless bright blue top, pale pants, earrings, and a large necklace. The woman is holding an Oikos drink bottle, while the man has an Oikos yogurt cup. They look concerned as the cable car appears stalled on the hill. An older woman with short reddish hair, large glasses, a pink floral top, a pale jacket, lavender pants, and a leopard-print bag sits beside the man, watching the situation. The young woman hands her Oikos bottle to the muscular man and moves toward the outside of the cable car. He ends up holding both his Oikos cup and her bottle as she climbs down from the side. The cable car’s maroon exterior is decorated with ornate gold lettering reading “O’Farrell & Hyde Jones Streets.” The woman braces both hands against the side panel and leans her whole body into it, pushing hard. Small white text appears near the bottom: “DRAMATIZATION. DO NOT ATTEMPT.” Her face tightens with effort as she strains against the cable car, her hair falling forward. Inside, passengers grip the poles and overhead rail as the cable car begins moving. From a low view near a stairway, the car is seen tilted on the incline, with the woman pushing from behind and the passengers riding inside. Back on the bench, the muscular man clutches the woman’s Oikos bottle and looks surprised, shifting in his seat as the car lurches. The older woman beside him turns her head toward him with wide eyes and an impressed, startled expression. In a nearby apartment window, a person in a striped robe and hair curlers looks down at the passing cable car while holding a spoon and cup, watching the strange scene through sheer curtains. The cable car rolls past a storefront sign reading “The Corner Market,” with smaller text advertising coffee and provisions in San Francisco. The cable car gains speed up the hill. On the sidewalk, road workers in reflective vests and hard hats stand beside orange traffic cones and a white vehicle as the cable car rushes past them. The young woman is then seen alone in the middle of the steep street, bent forward and breathing hard, with the tracks stretching behind her. She straightens and thrusts one arm upward, calling toward the cable car, her face urgent. Farther up the hill, the cable car continues away near the crest. At the rear of the cable car, the muscular man stands on the outside step holding the Oikos bottle out, with the San Francisco skyline and the tall, triangular Transamerica Pyramid behind him. He gestures broadly as if returning the bottle. The young woman stands far below near the top of the hill with both arms raised, and a small bottle arcs through the sky above her against the pale blue background and the Golden Gate Bridge. For a moment the road is empty except for the tracks and the bridge beyond. Then the woman pops back into view, hair flying upward from the movement, smiling with relief as she holds up the recovered Oikos bottle. She drinks from the Oikos protein shake bottle while standing on the sunny hillside street. Large bold white text appears to her left: “PROTEIN PACKED.” Fine print along the bottom says that protein and exercise help fuel strong muscles as part of a balanced diet and notes that it is not a low-calorie food.
