He has dark, combed hair and wears a light-colored suit jacket, dress shirt, and dark tie. His hands rest on the tops of the sets as he faces forward like a demonstrator. To his left is a larger television cabinet with a broad, rounded rectangular screen and controls beneath it. To his right is a darker, older-looking set with a much smaller screen area and speaker grilles on either side. The larger set begins showing a close-up of a young woman’s face in profile. She has dark, smooth hair and appears to be smiling or speaking, her head and shoulders filling much of the big rounded screen. The smaller set beside the man has a noticeably smaller blank screen, and a tiny floating image of the same woman’s head appears on the wall behind it, emphasizing the difference in viewing size. The man leans slightly toward the larger television and gestures over its screen. He then lifts a rounded rectangular panel or screen-shaped image upward from the large television. The panel contains the woman’s close-up, now separated from the TV cabinet like a visual comparison card. He holds it by the top edge, raising it beside his own head. The woman’s face on the panel is nearly as large as the man’s, making the comparison very direct. The big television cabinet below is now blank, while the small image remains off to the side in the background. The scene dissolves into a single RCA Victor television set placed in a home-like setting. The set stands on slim legs and has a large rounded screen with the same woman’s smiling profile displayed. Large white price lettering appears over the lower part of the set: “$199.95.” Beneath it, smaller text reads, “SLIGHTLY HIGHER IN FAR WEST AND SOUTH.” The price text then disappears, leaving the television centered with the woman’s close-up still on the screen. More of the living room becomes visible around the set. The television sits against the back wall, beneath three framed pictures. To the left are a sofa, curtains, a side table, a floor lamp, and an upholstered chair. In the foreground is a coffee table with magazines or papers and a dark floral arrangement. To the right are another chair, a small table or console, and a pair of matching lamps. The television remains the central object in the room. The woman’s image fades away, leaving the screen blank, and the set stands quietly as part of the furnished living space. Near the end, large translucent lettering begins to appear over the living room wall, then becomes a bold RCA Victor brand graphic. The room fades behind it. The final image is the RCA Victor logo on a plain background: large capital letters spelling “RCA VICTOR,” with the familiar dog sitting beside a phonograph horn, listening into it. Below, in quotation marks, the text reads “HIS MASTER’S VOICE.”

A black-and-white scene opens on a wall calendar hanging against a plain dark background. The visible page reads “1952,” “MAY,” a very large “30,” and “FRIDAY,” establishing the date. Beneath the calendar, a tabletop arrangement comes into view: a compact portable radio with a glossy dark rounded case and a pale front grille. The brand name “RCA Victor” is visible near the bottom of the radio’s front. To the radio’s right sits a small rectangular RCA battery carton with the RCA circle logo on its face. A pair of adult hands, seen from the wrists down in suit sleeves, begins handling the radio. One hand wears a ring. The hands steady the portable set and turn it so the plain dark back faces forward. The person’s fingers feel along the back panel and top edge, then open the rear of the radio. Inside, the radio’s components are exposed: a metal chassis across the top with small printed markings, rows of holes, wiring, and compact electrical parts arranged in the lower compartment. The hands work carefully inside the open radio, moving wires and reaching into the battery compartment. A rectangular RCA battery package is brought in from the right, its side showing a round RCA logo. The battery is guided into the lower part of the radio’s interior while the other hand holds loose leads and positions the connectors. The battery is slid into place horizontally across the bottom section, with the RCA logo facing outward. The fingers continue adjusting the wires, pressing them down and tucking them into the space around the battery so the parts sit neatly inside the open case. After the battery is installed, the radio is turned again so its smooth back faces outward. To the left of the radio, a retail display of RCA batteries appears on the tabletop. It includes a box with two upright cylindrical batteries pictured or standing on top, each carrying the RCA logo. A sign on the display reads “RCA” and “Radio A Battery.” The radio remains at the right edge while the battery display becomes the focus. The view then presents a wider assortment of RCA battery packages arranged like a store display. There are several rectangular cartons and cylindrical battery forms in different sizes, all marked with the RCA logo. Large boxes are stacked at the back, smaller boxes and open display trays sit in front, and the text “RADIO A B BATTERY” is visible on a large carton. Other packaging shows RCA logos and product labels for radio batteries, suggesting a variety of sizes for different portable radio models. The final close-up isolates two products: a large rectangular box on the left and a cylindrical battery on the right. Both carry bold RCA circle logos. The box reads “RADIO B BATTERY” and includes the line “RADIO-ENGINEERED FOR EXTRA LISTENING HOURS.” Below that, smaller text reads “No. VS 016 • 67½ VOLTS.” The cylindrical battery beside it is labeled “RADIO A BATTERY,” also with the RCA logo prominently centered. The commercial ends visually on this clear product display, emphasizing the branded RCA radio batteries and their packaging.

In black and white, the commercial begins in darkness with the front of a large, glossy automobile approaching or standing in a dim outdoor setting. Its two round headlights shine brightly on either side of a tall, formal grille, with reflections glinting across the hood and chrome trim. The car has the dignified look of a limousine. A white-gloved hand in a dark sleeve reaches for the door handle, and the person opening it wears a dark uniform with decorative cords or braid, suggesting a chauffeur or formal attendant. From beside the car, the attendant removes a rectangular, polished-looking presentation box. The box has a dark vertical panel on the front with a shield-like crest near the top, making it look like a ceremonial gift. The setting shifts to an elegant interior that resembles a palace or grand residence. A large chandelier hangs at the left, with candle-shaped lights and dangling glass ornaments. A suit of armor stands against the wall near a column, and the floor is laid out in large square tiles. A man in a light-colored formal uniform carries the presentation box through the hall. He approaches a richly furnished study or office where an older, light-haired man in a dark suit sits at a desk in a high-backed ornate chair. A table lamp glows behind the desk, and papers and desk objects lie in front of him. The uniformed man sets the gift box on the desk, facing the seated man, who leans forward with interest. The box is opened in front of him. Its top and front panels lift away, and inside is a portable radio. The uniformed man holds the open packaging steady while the seated man rises slightly from his chair and reaches toward the radio. The product is a Zenith Trans-Oceanic radio, a compact, suitcase-like rectangular set with a carrying handle on top. It has a dark front, shiny metal trim, a row of small tuning marks across the upper front, and a large round control knob. Hands lift the radio out of the box and place it on the desk for a closer look. A close view shows the radio centered on the desk. A hand rests on the handle at the top while another hand opens the front cover. As the cover drops down, it reveals the radio’s lighter speaker grille panel, horizontal tuning scales across the upper section, several small knobs on the left, and a large circular tuning dial on the lower right. The hands adjust the controls, turning a knob and moving over the tuning area, demonstrating how the portable radio opens and operates. The scene briefly returns to an overhead view of the desk, where the older man sits with the radio in front of him. The radio is then shown more prominently on its own, open and gleaming, with the Zenith name visible on the upper right of the front panel. Its handle stands upright, and the open front cover forms a base beneath it. The commercial then introduces smaller Zenith radios. A hand places a tiny pocket-sized transistor radio on a checkerboard or chessboard surface. The little radio stands upright among blurred chess pieces in the background. It has vertical grille bars on the front, a small display area near the top, and the word “ZENITH” clearly printed across its face. After the hand withdraws, the small radio remains centered, emphasizing how compact it is. Several Zenith radios are displayed together on a shelf or tabletop. They vary in size and shape: some are rectangular table models with broad speaker grilles, some have circular dials, and others are slim portable sets. White on-screen text appears near the bottom reading “FM/AM RADIOS.” The display changes to another group of larger household sets, including table radios and clock radios with clock faces and rectangular cabinets. The bottom text changes to “TABLE AND CLOCK RADIOS.” Another arrangement follows, showing portable radios of different sizes, including small transistor sets with wrist straps, medium portables with handles, and a larger portable with an extended antenna. The bottom text reads “SOLID STATE PORTABLES.” The display grows into a broad collection of many Zenith radios arranged in rows and at different heights, filling the scene from foreground to background. There are boxy radios with large round dials, slim rectangular models, handle-top portables, and clock radios, all presented together like a showroom lineup. Over this array, a large stylized “ZENITH” logo appears in bold white lettering with a lightning-like slash through the initial Z. Beneath it, cursive-style text fades in: “The quality goes in before the name goes on.” The final image settles on a smaller grouping of Zenith radios: a large Trans-Oceanic-style portable behind, a tiny pocket radio in front, and another portable radio at the right with a circular dial and raised antenna. The big Zenith logo remains above them, with the slogan underneath. An ornate picture-frame border appears around the whole display, as if the radios and logo are being presented as a framed gift or treasured object.

The commercial opens in black and white against a plain dark background. A compact rectangular television set is held up from underneath by an off-screen demonstrator’s hand, making it look small and portable, almost like a little suitcase. At first the darker back or side of the set faces forward, with a pair of round fittings or knobs near the center and a ribbed top surface visible. Large white block letters reading “NEW!” appear above it. The set is then turned to reveal its front: a rounded rectangular screen area framed by a thick cabinet. On the screen is the RCA Victor name in large lettering, with the familiar RCA circle and the small dog listening to a gramophone. A handle is visible on top. The same compact set is then held by its top handle, hanging in midair, and bold white text appears below it reading “Personal TV.” The product is shown more directly from the front, now set on a small detachable stand with crossed legs beneath it. A hand grips the top handle and steadies or adjusts the television as it sits on the stand. The screen continues to display the RCA Victor logo and dog-and-gramophone symbol. Small side knobs protrude from the cabinet, and the front frame has softly rounded corners. As the view moves closer, the screen fills more of the image, emphasizing the RCA Victor name and the compact cabinet surrounding it. The focus shifts to the top of the television. The top surface has two ribbed vented sections, one on each side, with a darker central strip or recessed channel running lengthwise between them. A pair of hands enters from above and pinches two thin metal rods hidden near the center. The hands pull the rods upward from the top of the set, revealing them as a built-in antenna. The rods rise vertically, then are drawn farther out and spread apart into a wide V shape, each hand holding one slender antenna arm. The scene changes to a domestic bedroom or dressing area. A skirted vanity table stands against the dark background, with a round-backed chair in front and a large oval mirror rising behind the tabletop. A young adult woman in a light-colored robe or housecoat sits at the vanity, seen mostly from behind and in profile, with her face visible in the mirror. She raises her arms as if arranging her hair or grooming at the mirror. A small RCA Victor Personal TV sits on the right side of the vanity table, angled toward her, its compact cabinet perched on its little stand. The arrangement suggests she can watch the set while seated at her dressing table. The image then blends into an office setting. An adult man with short dark hair, wearing a striped suit jacket, sits with his back to the viewer in an upholstered desk chair. In front of him is a desk with a rotary telephone on the left, a desk lamp near the middle, and the small RCA Victor television placed on the desk facing him. Heavy curtains hang along the left side. The man sits upright, then lifts a hand toward his face as if adjusting glasses or rubbing his temple, before lowering his arm toward the desk. The television remains positioned as a personal viewing set within easy reach on the desktop. Finally, the scene changes to a kitchen. A woman stands with her back to the viewer at a light-colored counter, wearing a short-sleeved checked dress and a white apron tied in a large bow at the back. Above the counter, pots and pans hang from a horizontal rack. The small television sits on the counter ahead of her, again on its stand and facing into the room. Cabinets and kitchen surfaces frame the space, and the woman’s posture suggests she can watch the compact set while working in the kitchen.

The commercial opens in black and white on the outside of a modern-looking dealership. Large block letters on a wall read “DE SOTO PLYMOUTH,” with a glass doorway beside the sign. The scene shifts into a simple, stylized animated world. A smiling cartoon man, presented like a mid-century office or city gentleman, stands in front of a tiled dealership wall. He wears a dark suit, white shirt, tie, and a tall dark hat. He gestures with one raised finger, then brings his hand toward his mouth as if speaking or making a point. A cartoon woman pops in beside him from the right, leaning close and putting a hand on his shoulder. She appears cheerful and glamorous, with a tilted dark hat or beret, earrings, a fitted dress, and exaggerated star-like eyelashes. Both characters smile broadly, facing forward as if addressing the viewer or someone just offscreen. A second animated man appears, this one dressed like a formal salesman or master of ceremonies in a dark tuxedo with a bow tie. On his chest is a round badge with ribbons that reads “1955 DeSoto.” He has a round face, small mustache-like marking, and a swoop of hair. He gestures expansively, lifting one finger, raising an arm high, and posing with theatrical enthusiasm. As he moves, an animated 1955 DeSoto comes into view inside a showroom-like setting. The car sits on a raised display area, with curtains draped behind it and a leafy potted plant at the left. The car has a long, low body, whitewall tires, prominent chrome at the front, and a two-tone side panel suggested by different shades of gray. The earlier man and woman enter from the left and approach the salesman. They stand near him, looking toward the car. The salesman seems to usher them along, gesturing eagerly. The group bunches together in front of the display, and the salesman’s excited movements push the action toward the right edge. He spins or dances aside, leaving the car as the main focus. The animated DeSoto remains centered on the showroom platform, framed by the curtain and plant, then rolls away to the right. A circular sign appears against a brick wall with the words “1955 DeSoto.” The circle opens visually into a front view of the real car, transitioning from animation into live-action footage. The car faces forward, centered against a plain light background at first. Its broad chrome grille, rounded headlights, hood ornament, and front license plate are prominent. The plate reads “ZX 44843.” The car then appears driving toward the viewer on a wide open road, with a flat horizon and distant landscape behind it. The chrome grille and bumper catch the light, and the windshield shows occupants inside. The DeSoto is shown from multiple angles while driving. From the side, it is a long, low two-door car with a hardtop roofline, large whitewall tires, and a sweeping contrasting side treatment along the body. From the rear three-quarter angle, its fins, rear lights, trunk shape, and wide rear bumper are visible as it moves away along the road. The setting is open and spacious, like a highway or test road, with little traffic and a broad sky. The commercial returns to animation. A group of cartoon pedestrians stands along a city sidewalk in front of a wall. They are drawn in varied shapes and styles: a short person with round glasses and a brimmed hat, a tall narrow man with a long face, a woman in a fitted light dress and wide-brimmed hat, and others clustered behind them. Their bodies face the street and their heads turn as a DeSoto passes across the foreground from right to left. They appear to stop and look, smiling or staring with interest as the car goes by. After it passes, the group remains gathered, still oriented toward where the car went. A stylized residential street appears, with several houses lined up side by side. The houses have sharp triangular roofs, square windows, bare trees, and a flat sidewalk in front. A DeSoto drives into view along the street and stops or slows in front of the homes. As it appears, people begin showing up in the windows and doorways: figures lean out from upstairs and downstairs windows, a person stands on an upper balcony or porch, and others peer from neighboring houses. Their heads and upper bodies angle toward the car. The DeSoto sits below them at curb level, its side profile visible, again with the long body, whitewall tires, and sweeping two-tone side design. The car visually becomes the center of attention in the neighborhood scene. The view changes to the real car’s interior. A large pale steering wheel fills the left side, with a shiny chrome-and-metal dashboard stretching across the frame. The instrument panel has several round gauges and dials arranged in a balanced, cockpit-like layout. The surfaces are glossy and reflective. A close view emphasizes a small control lever mounted on the dashboard near the gauges, projecting outward from a chrome base. This appears to be the feature identified in the commercial context as the “flight control lever.” The lever sits conveniently near the driver’s side controls, with surrounding knobs and circular instruments visible. The image dissolves back to the animated neighborhood, where the DeSoto remains parked or displayed at the curb. Cartoon people stand around it: a man at the left, a person near the rear, and a woman at the right in a skirt or dress. The car’s side is emphasized, especially the dramatic contrasting sweep along the body that starts near the front and flows rearward. In black and white, the “color sweep” reads as a bold lighter-and-darker slash across the side panels. The real DeSoto returns on the open road, now shown in a front three-quarter view. It moves smoothly across the pavement with the horizon behind it. Its chrome grille, hood ornament, rounded headlights, whitewall tires, and contrasting side sweep are all visible. Large cursive on-screen writing appears over the road scene, reading “Smartest of the Smart Cars.” The word “Smartest” stretches widely above the car, while “of the Smart Cars” appears below in flowing script. The text fades, leaving the car continuing along the highway. The final views return to the car in motion from the side. The DeSoto travels steadily across a flat, open landscape, its long profile and low stance clearly shown. The hardtop roof, broad rear fender, whitewall wheels, and sweeping side trim remain visible as the commercial ends with the automobile moving confidently along the road.

A black-and-white image opens on a large tabletop radio, filling most of the screen. Its front is divided into two wide grille sections with horizontal slats, a tuning dial with numbers across the lower middle, and two round knobs near the bottom corners. Behind and above it are leafy plants or flowers, giving the radio a domestic, decorative setting. The radio image fades into a poised young adult woman facing forward in an elegant studio interior. She has carefully set, waved hair, light-toned skin, arched brows, and a polished 1950s look. She wears a dark, off-the-shoulder dress with a light trim along the neckline, a double strand of pearls, matching earrings, and bracelets. Draped curtains hang to one side, and an ornate wall sconce or chandelier detail appears on the other, suggesting a formal dressing-room or parlor-like setting. She speaks directly outward, her expression composed and knowing, then smiles slightly as if offering advice. She reaches down and lifts a bottle or can of hair product into view. She presents it beside her face, supporting it with one hand and gesturing toward it with the other. The container is light-colored with a small spray-style top and a printed label; the large visible words on the front read “SATIN-SET,” with “Revlon” written below in script. She holds it steady so the label faces outward, then continues speaking with the product raised beside her. Her posture is upright and confident, and the product is treated as the main object of attention. The scene changes to another young adult woman with light-toned skin and light blonde hair, seated or standing before a background of louvered shutters. She wears an off-the-shoulder lace-patterned dress, pearl earrings, and a bracelet. Her hair is styled in soft curls, but at first the curls at the side and back appear loose and drooping. She turns her head slightly to one side and touches the ends of her hair near her neck, looking concerned and uncertain. Her eyebrows lift and her mouth tightens into a worried expression as she fingers the limp curl. Large bold white letters appear to her right reading “WATER,” visually identifying the ordinary setting method being contrasted. She continues to touch the sagging side curl while looking off to the side, her expression suggesting disappointment with how the hairstyle is holding. Her expression then changes. She turns more toward the front, relaxes, and smiles as the hair around her face appears neater and more formed. The curls at the sides and back look fuller, more defined, and springy. She turns her head from front to side, smiling broadly, as if showing that the curls keep their shape from different angles. She lifts a hand to the side of her head and lightly pats or fluffs the curl cluster near her ear. On the left side of the screen, large bold lettering appears in quotation marks: “‘SATIN-SET’.” While that text remains, she continues to touch and display the curls, smiling and glancing to the side. The visual comparison is clear: the earlier “WATER” hair looked limp and worrying, while the “SATIN-SET” hair looks smooth, arranged, and resilient. The elegant presenter returns in the formal interior. She again raises the Satin-Set container beside her, label facing forward. Across the lower part of the image, large bold white text appears: “NO LACQUER.” The product remains in her hand at the left side of her body while she speaks outward. After the text fades, she lowers the container and gestures with her free hand up toward the back of her own neatly set hair, lightly touching it behind her ear. Her hair stays smooth and carefully waved as she smiles, then brings her hand down and continues addressing the viewer. Near the end, the presenter remains centered while a large product image and lettering begin to appear behind and over her. The final product display takes over: on the left is an enlarged bottle of Revlon Satin-Set, with a cap and a patterned label that prominently reads “SATIN-SET” and “Revlon.” On the right, bold white lettering reads “Revlon ‘SATIN-SET’ PIN-CURL SPRAY-SET,” with “Revlon” in a cursive script above the block letters. The background becomes dark and plain, making the bottle and text stand out clearly. In the final view, the bottle stays on the left while new large white words on the right read: “SET PIN-CURLS THAT LAST TWICE AS LONG!”

A black-and-white Ford crest fills the screen, with the word “FORD” in large block letters at the top of a shield-shaped emblem. As the emblem fades, it remains superimposed over the front side of a parked 1957 Ford Fairlane. The car sits in a driveway beside a mid-century suburban house with brickwork, large windows, shrubs, and flower beds. The Fairlane is a two-tone hardtop with a light roof and light rear side panel, darker body sides, chrome trim, whitewall tires, and shiny hubcaps. A man in a dark suit and dress shoes walks alongside the car carrying two hard-sided suitcases, one in each hand. Only his lower body and hands are seen at first. He passes the front wheel and continues toward the rear of the car. The side of the Ford fills the view, showing its long, smooth body line, chrome door handle, and the distinctive sweeping two-tone panel that curves toward the rear fins. At the trunk, a close view shows the rear lock and trim. The word “FAIRLANE” is visible on the trunk ornament beneath a round lock. The man’s hand holds a key, inserts it into the lock, and turns it. The trunk lid lifts open. Inside, the trunk is spacious, with a patterned floor mat and a full-size spare tire standing upright at the back. A California license plate reading “MRT 031” is mounted on the lowered rear panel. The man places a large suitcase into the trunk, sliding it flat inside, then adds a second suitcase on top of it. The luggage fits beneath the raised trunk lid, beside the spare tire. With the luggage stowed, the scene returns to the car’s side. The suited man walks forward along the driver’s side toward the door. He reaches for the chrome handle, pulls it, and the door opens outward. The interior is visible through the open door: a broad front seat, the steering wheel, and the dashboard. He bends and slides into the driver’s seat, then begins pulling the door closed behind him. Inside the car, attention shifts to the controls. A chrome switch panel is set into quilted door trim; a finger presses one of several small switches. The window beside it is seen with blurred bushes outside, suggesting the glass is being operated. Another close view shows the side of the front seat, where the man’s hand reaches down to a small control near the seat base, indicating an adjustment to the powered seat. His suit sleeve and shirt cuff are visible as he works the control. The rear of the Fairlane appears, highlighting the round taillight set into the tail fin, the broad chrome bumper, and the clean, symmetrical rear styling. The car backs away from the house along the driveway, growing smaller as it moves into the open space. The suburban setting remains visible: a low-roofed house to the right, flower beds beneath the windows, and trees in the background. The viewpoint moves to inside the car, looking forward through the windshield over the dashboard. A quiet residential street stretches ahead with lawns, trees, and houses. A boy rides a bicycle near the curb ahead of the car. The Ford then appears from behind on the street, its white roof, rear fins, round taillights, and whitewall tires clearly visible as it drives past neat houses and landscaped yards. A close view shows the boy’s face as he moves along outdoors. He appears to be a preteen or young teenage boy with light skin, dark wavy hair combed back, and a jacket over a collared shirt. He looks toward the passing car with a slight smile, then purses his lips as if whistling or reacting with interest, before smiling again. The background behind him is blurred foliage and sidewalk, reinforcing that he is moving. Inside the Ford again, a dashboard clock is shown in close detail, with a rectangular face and large numbers around it. Then the radio fills the view. Its horizontal dial is marked with numbers from about 5.5 through 16, with a row of push buttons beneath. A finger presses one of the preset buttons. The radio dial then dissolves into a view of an open road, visually linking the dashboard controls to the driving scene. A smooth, empty highway curves gently through a wooded area. Trees line both sides, and the pale road surface sweeps to the right. The car itself is not visible in this part; the view suggests traveling forward along a quiet, open road. The Ford appears again from the side on a rural highway. The camera stays close to the front fender and door area as the car moves, showing the chrome side trim, whitewall front tire, and the “Fairlane” script along the front side panel. Fields, low hills, and distant trees slide by in the background. The driver, still in a dark suit, is visible through the open side window with his hands near the steering wheel. As the view moves rearward along the car, the sweeping two-tone side panel and white roof stand out, followed by the rear quarter, tail fin, round taillight, and chrome bumper. The Fairlane continues cruising along a straight open highway. From behind and slightly to the side, its rear styling is prominent: twin round taillights, broad bumper, central trunk ornament, and wide rear window. The car remains steady in its lane, with open countryside, scattered trees, and low mountains in the distance. Near the end, the Ford is seen head-on driving along a road through a wide landscape. Its front grille spans the width of the car, with round headlights set high at each side and chrome bumper guards below. The road and distant hills frame the car. The Ford crest then appears over the center of the grille and enlarges until it dominates the screen, again showing the bold “FORD” name at the top of the shield.

The commercial opens in black and white with a large white letter Q encircling a stylized face in a dark hat and white collar against a plain background. This graphic dissolves into a home kitchen, where large white title lettering appears over the scene: “Aunt Jemima presents Peggy and Chuck,” with “Peggy” and “Chuck” written in a script style. Behind the lettering, a tidy kitchen is visible with a refrigerator at the back, cupboards, a windowed door on the right, and a counter in the foreground holding a griddle, pans, dishes, and an Aunt Jemima pancake mix box. As the title fades, a young adult woman stands at the kitchen counter. She wears a light-colored, short-sleeved house dress or blouse with a belted waist, and her dark hair is neatly styled short. She holds a tall cylindrical container, shaking or handling it as if mixing pancake batter. On the counter beside her are cooking items, including a flat griddle, a small pan, a bowl, and ingredients laid out near the Aunt Jemima box. A young adult man enters from the right holding a baby. He wears a darker shirt tucked into light trousers. The baby, in a patterned outfit, is held upright against his chest. The woman turns toward them, smiles, and gestures toward the child, briefly reaching out as if including the baby in the conversation, then turns back to the counter to continue explaining or preparing the food. The view shifts to a close look at the griddle. Four pale apple rings, each shaped like a small doughnut with a hole in the center, sit spaced apart on the hot surface. A woman’s hand tilts a tall mixing container over the griddle while another hand holds a spoon nearby. Thick, light pancake batter pours from the container onto one apple ring, spreading into a round pancake shape around it. She moves from one ring to another, pouring batter so that the apple slices become centered inside the pancake batter. The batter pools and spreads in smooth circles, leaving some rings still visible and others partly covered. The scene then moves to a round breakfast table in the same kitchen. The woman sits on the left, the man on the right, and the baby sits between them in a high chair. The table is set with plates, cups, a small pitcher of dark syrup, and breakfast food. The man lifts food with a fork and eats from his plate, while the woman sits with a pleasant expression and reaches for items on the table. The baby leans forward in the high chair, occupied with food or a cup. The woman pours dark syrup from a small pitcher, and the man reaches toward the table, then picks up a folded newspaper or printed leaflet with pictures on it. He opens it and reads while still seated at breakfast. The woman continues eating and serving, glancing toward the baby, while the baby raises a cup or food toward the mouth. The family appears relaxed and domestic, gathered around the breakfast table. The commercial returns to a cooking demonstration at the counter. An Aunt Jemima pancake mix box is clearly visible on the left, showing the brand name and a portrait-style logo of a smiling woman in a head scarf, along with an image of pancakes on the front. A flat electric griddle sits in the center, with a control dial on the left edge. To the right is a metal bowl holding apple rings, and behind the griddle are a tall mixing container and small bowls. A hand uses a spatula to lift apple rings from the metal bowl and place them on the griddle. The rings are set down one by one, spaced apart in a neat arrangement, then adjusted with the spatula as if sautéing them. After several apple rings are arranged on the griddle, the batter container is tilted over them again. Thick pancake batter pours in a steady stream onto and around the apple rings. A spoon held in the other hand helps control the batter. Some batter forms plain round pancakes nearby, while other pours cover the apple rings so the rings sit centered inside the pancakes. The griddle surface shows several pale circles cooking at once. A finished serving plate appears on a woven placemat. The commercial begins with a wintry, graphic holiday scene: a dark, starry background filled with bright white snowflakes of different sizes, sparkling points of light, and floating shapes that look like tiny handheld game screens. In the middle of the snowflake pattern, red-orange lettering appears inside a pale, glowing oval. As the snowflakes drift and overlap, the words resolve into a festive Radio Shack Christmas message, with “Radio Shack” and “The Technology Store” suggested in the glowing holiday graphic. The scene shifts to a cozy living room decorated for Christmas. An elderly white man with a bald head, white hair at the sides, and a white mustache sits facing forward in a plaid upholstered chair. He wears a dark red cardigan over a plaid shirt and scarf-like collar. A table lamp with a pleated shade glows beside him, and behind him are patterned blue wallpaper, shelves, candles, and holiday decorations. He looks alert and slightly mischievous, as if about to explain or demonstrate something. In a softly lit child’s bedroom, a young girl with light brown hair tied back with a large pink bow sits at a white desk doing schoolwork in an open book. She wears a pale blue sweater with large white cloudlike patches. The elderly man stands behind her, leaning forward with a small rectangular handheld electronic game in both hands. He lifts it up near his face, then moves quietly away while the girl continues writing, mostly unaware. The room has a pale table lamp, framed wall art, shelves with small toys or dolls, and hats hanging on the wall, giving it a warm, domestic feel. The man carries the handheld game to the nearby bed and sets it down on a flat surface at the bedside. Stuffed animals sit at the foot of the bed. He bends over it with intense concentration, then sits down and brings both hands over the controls, his posture hunched and focused like a child absorbed in play. A close view of the game shows a space-themed design: illustrated spacecraft around a central rectangular LCD screen, small orange buttons below, and a digital score that changes from around 90 to 100. The screen shows a corridor-like space scene with tiny dark shapes, suggesting enemies or targets moving through a futuristic tunnel. Back in the living room, a middle-aged white man in a white sweater and light trousers sits on a plaid sofa holding a newspaper. He smiles as the elderly man enters from the left and places another small handheld game on the wooden coffee table. The room is festive, with a Christmas tree visible to one side, a lamp, books, magazines, a red candle, and garland. The elderly man crouches at the coffee table and begins playing the dark-colored game, pressing buttons with both hands while the seated man watches with amusement. A close view shows the game labeled with a jet-fighter theme; the body is dark gray or black, with a small raised screen, a yellow “FIRE” button, and smaller controls marked “LOCK” and “SET.” The LCD display shows aircraft silhouettes and target-like shapes, matching the jet-fighter imagery. The elderly man then appears in a kitchen or dining area with warm yellow curtains over windows and a wooden table. He picks up a larger turquoise-and-blue handheld electronic game from a table or counter. A woman with curly brown hair, wearing a white blouse, dark vest, and long pink skirt, stands in the background with a young boy in a blue sweatshirt; they seem to be sharing or holding a cup while watching from the side. The man walks toward the table, holding the game with both hands and looking down at it, then sets it in front of him and plays. A close view reveals a football-themed handheld game, decorated with illustrated football players in yellow and blue uniforms around a central LCD screen, with orange control buttons below. The screen shows small moving football-field figures. The family gathers together in the living room around the elderly man. He sits in the center on the sofa, still in his red cardigan, while the young girl kneels or stands at the coffee table on his left and a young boy in a bright blue sweatshirt sits to his right. Behind them, the middle-aged man in the white sweater and the curly-haired woman lean over the back of the couch, smiling. The Christmas tree, garland, patterned wallpaper, lamp, and red candle remain visible, making the room feel festive and crowded with family attention. The girl finishes playing with a small handheld game and turns toward the elderly man. She hands him a small yellow electronic game. He receives it with both hands, his face opening into delight, then looks down and starts pressing its controls. The children and adults watch him closely, smiling and laughing. He reacts with a wide open-mouthed grin, lifting the yellow game slightly as if proudly showing it off, while everyone leans in around him. The commercial ends with a product display on a plain light surface against a dark background. A wide assortment of Radio Shack electronic games is arranged in a semicircle: several small handheld units in green, white, yellow, black, blue, and gray; a larger tabletop-style game with a grid of colored squares; and other compact electronic toys and game cards. Large white on-screen text at the top reads, “From $7.95 to $29.95.” Smaller white text at the bottom reads, “Batteries Not Included.”

A warmly lit office appears, with mustard-yellow walls, venetian-blind shadows, framed artwork, and a desk holding early-1980s office equipment: a printer and a beige CRT computer terminal. In the foreground, a light-skinned adult woman with short, curly dark hair sits or leans forward at her desk with her back partly to view. She wears a pale gray blazer over a white blouse with a soft scarf-like bow at the neck. In the doorway across the room stands an older light-skinned man, balding with hair at the sides, wearing large glasses, a dark suit, tie, and pocket square. He faces into the office as if addressing her, then steps slightly inward and turns his head toward the computer equipment beside him. The woman is then seen from the front, smiling up toward the older man. Her expression is polite and attentive at first, and she leans forward beside a wooden desk partition. Behind her, striped light from blinds falls across the wall, and a framed picture hangs to her left. As the exchange continues, her smile softens into a more uncertain, dutiful look. The older man appears in close view, his large glasses prominent, his face serious. He turns his head aside, then leaves through the doorway. The door or wall edge fills the view as he passes out, briefly obscuring him. Attention moves to the portable computer. A pair of hands places a compact white Radio Shack Model 100 Portable Computer into an open brown briefcase on a desktop. The machine is rectangular, with a full black keyboard on the lower half, a long narrow display screen above it, and small control panels on the right. Around it are office items: a small potted cactus, stacked binders or folders, a black notebook, a pen, and a desk nameplate that appears to identify Fletcher. The hands settle the computer neatly into the briefcase, then the briefcase lid begins to close over it, emphasizing that the computer can be packed up and carried. The woman is then shown away from the office, sitting in the back seat of a car or taxi beside a window. She now wears a beige trench coat and holds the Model 100 on a small wooden surface in front of her. City scenery outside the car window passes by in soft blur. She looks down, positions the computer in front of her, and begins using it, resting one hand near the keyboard and the other near the side of the machine. Her posture is focused and businesslike, using the computer as a traveling workstation. The setting changes again to a home-like room with warm wood tones. A sofa sits in the background, with a side table holding a cream-colored telephone. A coffee table is cluttered with papers, a cup, and small objects. The same dark-haired person, likely Fletcher, sits forward over the Model 100 on the coffee table, typing and working intently. The room includes a lamp and dark furniture in the background, giving the sense of a comfortable living room being used as an office. A close view shows hands typing rapidly on the Model 100’s black keys. The long display screen shows faint lines of text, though the words are not readable. A pair of eyeglasses and papers lie above the computer on the table. The hands continue working across the keyboard, demonstrating it as a word processor or general work machine. Then an arm wearing a wristwatch reaches past the computer toward telephone equipment. Beside the computer are cords, a black acoustic coupler-like device, and a cream push-button telephone. A white handset is lifted and placed into the black cradle, with cords running between the phone equipment and the workspace, visually suggesting the portable computer connecting through the telephone line. Back in the office, the older man returns through the doorway. He is now without his suit jacket, wearing a dark vest over his dress shirt and tie, and carrying papers. He steps into the office where the printer and CRT terminal sit on the table against the yellow wall. Papers are scattered on the desk, and a red-orange object or garment rests in the foreground. Fletcher herself is not clearly visible here, making the office feel momentarily unattended as he looks in. The product is then displayed alone on a dark background. The Model 100 sits angled upward with a pen beside it, its white body, black keyboard, and long display clearly visible. Large white on-screen text reads “From $799.” Beneath it, a higher price, “$1,099,” is shown crossed out, reinforcing the sale price. Finally, a black background holds a rectangular picture of the older man seated in the office, reading a sheet of paper beside the printer and CRT computer. Large red text below reads “Radio Shack,” and white text underneath says “Model 100 now on sale.”

A busy, slightly comic office scene opens on a dark-haired, middle-aged man seated behind an overflowing desk. He wears a white shirt, dark vest, and tie, and his workspace is packed with papers, trays, notebooks, wires, rods, and odd homemade communication devices. A green banker-style hanging lamp glows above him. Around him are metal tubes and horn-shaped speaking devices, including a large flared horn over his left shoulder and several mechanical arms stretching across the desk. He has more than one telephone receiver crowded around his head and neck, and he looks harried as he tries to manage calls and signals at once. He sits forward with one receiver to his ear, then reaches across the desk toward the right, where a colorful panel of buttons, cords, and levers sits among the clutter. He grabs a yellow handset-like object, speaks into or toward it, then drops it back down. Still wearing receivers around his neck and against his ear, he turns toward a wall of devices beside a window. He points and gestures as if trying to direct a message through the improvised setup. Frustration builds visually: he raises both hands, then reaches up toward the metal speaking horn above him, as though calling through it. The view shifts to another office worker at a separate crowded desk. This man is fair-haired, wears glasses, a white shirt, suspenders, and a dark bow tie. He sits under a metal desk lamp, surrounded by stacks of paper, trays, pencils, and another flared speaking horn aimed at him from the left. As he reacts to the incoming message, loose sheets lift and flutter, and his hair is blown straight upward, making him look startled and overwhelmed. He looks toward the horn, then down at the papers in his hands, trying to cope with the disorderly system. Back at the first man’s desk, the dark-haired man continues with a black phone receiver pressed to one ear and another white receiver hanging around his neck. He raises the brass-colored horn with one hand, then lowers it while still talking. His expression is tense and intent. He works both receivers, then steadies himself at the desk. He turns to his right and reaches toward a small control on a wall-mounted contraption near a clear enclosure. A close view shows his hand pushing or pulling a small lever with a red knob beside a transparent pigeon compartment. Inside the clear box, a pigeon stands on a small perch. Large black lettering on the glass reads “CHICAGO” near the upper level and “DENVER” near the lower level. The hand moves the lever between the marked destinations, suggesting a makeshift message-routing system involving the bird. The improvised apparatus fades into a clean product display. On a wooden desk sits the AT&T Merlin telephone: a black-and-white business phone with a black handset on the left, a numeric keypad, and many rectangular programmable buttons arranged in columns. Beside it is a matching light-colored AT&T system box with a yellow band and AT&T markings. Papers and a document holder sit in the background, but the phone and box are centered and uncluttered. A hand reaches in and lifts the black handset from the Merlin phone, then points to the buttons. The display shows many labeled keys. In close-up, some labels are readable: “HENDERSON,” “LOUISE,” “INTERCOM,” “Conf/Trans,” and “Drop,” along with city or line labels such as “ST. LOUIS” and “BANK.” Small triangular indicator lights sit beside several buttons. The finger presses a button labeled “INTERCOM,” then moves down toward function keys such as “Conf/Trans,” visually demonstrating that calls and internal communication can be selected directly from the phone. A dark control unit appears next, shown as a black panel inside a cabinet or equipment rack. A hand reaches in and turns or adjusts a row of small controls on the front. The image briefly overlaps with the previous office scene, connecting the phone on the desk to the behind-the-scenes system equipment. The fair-haired man with glasses is now in a calmer, neater office. He sits at a clean desk under the same style of metal lamp, writing on a pad. A black Merlin phone rests to his left. Instead of reacting to horns and flying papers, he simply reaches to the phone, lifts the handset, and places it to his ear while continuing to hold his pencil. His posture is more composed, and the work surface is orderly. The scene changes to a more polished executive-style office. A dark-haired man in a gray suit and red tie sits at a large wooden desk beneath a green hanging lamp. He holds a black telephone receiver to his ear while reading a sheet of paper. A Merlin phone sits angled on the right side of his desk. The room has a framed landscape print on the wall, vertical blinds by a window, a vase with white flowers, and tidy desktop accessories. As he continues the call, he leans back in his chair and eventually puts his feet up on the desk, looking relaxed while still holding the receiver. On the left side of the room, a large birdcage appears, containing a dark bird perched inside. The cage grows more prominent as the executive remains on the phone, visually recalling the earlier pigeon-delivery gag but now in a calmer, controlled setting. Then a blue, glowing striped sphere begins to appear over the office scene. It expands and becomes the familiar AT&T globe logo, while the office fades into darkness behind it. The commercial ends on a black background with the blue AT&T globe above large white “AT&T” lettering. Beneath the logo, a bold white phone number fills the lower part of the screen: “1-800-247-7000.”

The commercial begins in darkness, then a soft, misty white studio space appears. In the center is a cream-colored Apple Macintosh computer: a compact, upright all-in-one machine with a small dark screen at the top, a narrow floppy disk slot below it, a separate low keyboard in front, and a small rectangular mouse off to the right, attached by a thin cord. The computer is presented alone, cleanly lit, with no people visible. The Macintosh slowly shifts from an ordinary exterior view into a cutaway, as if the casing has opened to reveal what is inside. The keyboard and mouse remain nearby while the computer’s side and back seem to peel away or become transparent. Inside, the machine becomes a colorful, miniature mechanical landscape. Curving red, yellow, blue, and black wires loop across the interior like thick vines or roads. Pale molded plastic parts, round components, brackets, and circuit-board structures fill the space. The view moves deeper through this interior, passing under and around arched cables and small electronic parts, with green and gold light giving everything a dreamlike, futuristic glow. The inner workings are shown in close detail. Thick orange and yellow cables sweep across the foreground, partially blocking and then revealing pale support pieces, dark connectors, and patterned circuit-board walls behind them. The shapes are not just plain hardware; they are arranged almost like a tiny city or factory inside the computer, with upright black pieces, rounded housings, slots, and pathways layered at different depths. The parts remain still, but the movement through them makes the interior feel large and complex. The view then glides over a flat green circuit board. Rows of tiny white dots and solder points form neat lines along both sides, while small yellow and orange components sit like markers along a central path. A large rectangular chip-like piece appears ahead, followed by additional black rectangular components with many evenly spaced metal pins underneath, standing like bridges or gates across the board. The circuit board surface is marked with fine printed lines and small white labels, though most of the tiny lettering is too indistinct to read. A round speaker-like part appears near the top of the image: a circular frame with a central cone and curved supports, mounted above the green board. Around it are small red and gold components and white printed circuit markings. The circular piece fills more of the view, then dissolves back into a broader look at the board, where many black chips, silver pins, and small upright parts are spread across the surface. The green board is dense with components, arranged in rows and clusters. The passage continues between tall, comb-like rows of metal pins and colored wires. Red, blue, purple, green, and orange cables run lengthwise, framing rows of gold and silver contacts. The parts are shown in close-up, with the metallic pins forming repeating vertical patterns. The interior remains abstract and magnified, emphasizing the complexity of the electronics rather than showing a person using them. Near the end of this internal journey, a pale cylindrical connector or shaft appears, set between rounded plastic housings. It points toward the right, glowing softly in the warm green-yellow light. This mechanical detail fills the screen, then the imagery dissolves back out to the complete Macintosh in the white studio setting. The cream computer, keyboard, and mouse are again visible as a simple desktop setup, with the mouse placed to the right and its cord trailing back toward the machine. The screen of the Macintosh briefly shows a simple graphic shape, faint and gray, resembling a folded envelope or slanted icon. The computer then fades away from view, leaving the mouse isolated against the soft white background. The mouse is cream-colored, rounded rectangular, with a single dark rectangular button on top and three small dark slits near one end. A light-skinned adult hand enters, gently taking hold of the mouse. The fingers wrap around it, and then the image cuts closer to a single fingertip poised above the mouse button. In extreme close view, the fingertip presses the one rectangular button downward. As the finger rests on the button, the word “Macintosh” appears over the image in large white serif lettering, centered on the screen. The background darkens behind the text until only the clean white “Macintosh” name remains on a dark field.

A man in a light gray suit jacket, dark shirt, and tie sits in a dark studio-like setting beside a computer game setup. He has curly light-brown hair and faces slightly toward the viewer while raising one hand to point over his shoulder at a monitor behind him. The monitor displays a colorful, blocky computer game screen: a maze-like layout with blue and green platforms and corridors, suggesting an action or puzzle game. Beneath the monitor is a beige computer keyboard or console unit, and to the right sits a small game box or cartridge package with a bright illustrated label. A white on-screen caption at the bottom identifies the speaker as “President” and, in larger letters, “BRODERBUND.” The dark background keeps attention on the man, the game screen, and the Atari XE-style computer game equipment he is presenting.

The commercial opens in a dark, steamy shower environment, lit so that water and wet skin gleam against a nearly black background. A bare hand and forearm reach up into a strong stream of water. The fingers are spread and slightly curved, with the water striking the palm and wrist and bursting outward in bright sprays and droplets. The stream runs down the arm, tracing the shape of the wrist and forearm. A chrome-and-black showerhead appears, angled downward, sending out several forceful streams. Its metal surface is shiny and faceted, with black bands around it; small lettering on the head identifies spray settings, including “CENTER SPRAY.” The product is presented as a substantial bathroom fixture with multiple water outlets. A light-skinned adult woman with short, dark, slicked-back wet hair is shown showering. She is bare-shouldered, with only her upper body visible. Water rushes across her face and shoulder as she leans sideways into the spray. Her eyes are closed, and her expression is relaxed, almost absorbed in the sensation. She tilts her head back under the falling water, exposing her neck and jawline while droplets scatter across her face and hair. The water continues to hit her from above and behind, forming bright streaks and bursts around her head. She turns so that her face is partly in shadow, then the stream catches the side of her neck and shoulder. Her posture remains slow and languid, as if enjoying the water pressure. Her hands then press and slide over her wet shoulder and upper back. One hand moves across the rounded shoulder while another steadies near the side of her body, suggesting she is massaging herself as the spray hits. The water beads on her skin and runs in sheets down her arm and back. Another product close-up follows, showing the same chrome-and-black showerhead pouring out a broad, bright flow. The woman leans her head to one side, eyes closed, with one hand spread over the back of her shoulder. Water crosses diagonally over her face, ear, neck, and shoulder. She rubs along the shoulder and upper back with slow, open-palmed strokes. A separate close view of her hand shows water streaming along her fingers and down the side of her body, emphasizing the force and texture of the spray. She bends forward slightly, one hand resting on her shoulder while water sweeps over the back of her neck. Her wet hair lies close to her head. She continues to move her hand over her shoulder and collarbone area, then tilts her chin upward into the water, her mouth slightly open and her face partly shadowed. The lighting keeps the background dark while the water flashes white around her. More close views show her hands sliding over her torso and side, the skin glossy with water. The spray splashes strongly against her body, then the view returns to her face from the side. She raises an arm above or across her head, and water falls over her forehead, nose, and cheeks. Her eyes remain closed, and her expression stays calm and pleasurable as droplets break across her face. The water continues to run over the side of her neck and shoulder. A lock or dark strand of wet hair hangs near her jaw as she turns slightly, and her fingers move near her face and hair. The spray strikes near her mouth and chin, then splashes down onto her shoulder. The showerhead is shown again in detail. A hand reaches up to the fixture and appears to adjust the ring or dial around the head. The visible setting reads “CENTER SPRAY,” and the water changes into many straight, evenly spaced streams pouring downward in a dense curtain. The hand remains near the side of the head as the water pattern continues. After more dark, partial views of her wet body, one leg is lifted into the spray. A hand strokes along the shin and calf while water streams over the leg and foot. The foot extends forward with toes pointed, and droplets fall from the heel and arch. The leg is rim-lit against the dark background, with the spray crossing behind it in pale diagonal lines. The hand glides down toward the ankle and foot, continuing the massage-like motion as water runs off in rivulets. The woman’s face returns, bent forward with one hand at the side of her neck and shoulder. Her eyes are closed or lowered, and she rubs her neck and upper chest while the spray passes across her face and body. She appears relaxed and focused on the feel of the water. The showerhead appears once more, held or adjusted by a wet hand. The same chrome-and-black fixture pours out a full pattern of streams, then shifts to stronger central jets. The product label on the head includes the Shower Massage branding, and the black band with white lettering remains visible. Near the end, water runs over a bent leg or arm while a hand rests on the skin, continuing the visual theme of self-massage under the spray. The woman’s face appears again in soft, wet close view, eyes closed, with one hand against her shoulder. The final image overlays a product logo on top of the dark shower scene. In a rectangular box near the lower center, white text reads “THE ORIGINAL” above a large script “Shower Massage,” with “BY TELEDYNE” underneath. Behind the logo, the woman’s wet arm and face remain partially visible in shadow, with water still falling around her.

At first, a compact shower radio hangs against glossy light-blue bathroom tiles. A wet hand reaches up and turns the black control knobs on its white lower panel. The unit has a black ribbed front, a white “Splash Dance” script logo near the top, a rectangular radio tuning scale in the middle, and three round knobs along the bottom labeled for volume, band, and tuning. It hangs by two dark straps from the shower pipe, close to a white showerhead spraying water. A young adult woman with wet, slicked-back brown hair stands under the spray beside the radio. Only her bare shoulders and upper chest are visible, as in a shower setting. She smiles broadly, dimples showing, and leans toward the water while facing the radio. She raises a hand near her face, then touches the controls and gestures as if keeping time. Water runs over her cheeks and neck. She turns her face into the spray, closes her eyes, and rubs water through her hair with one hand, looking relaxed and playful. The radio remains hanging just to her right, water droplets visible on its black front but the controls and tuning window still clear. The view moves closer to the woman’s face and ear as she rubs her wet hair and then lowers her hand. She tilts her chin upward under the shower stream, then moves forward so the radio is centered behind her. The “Splash Dance” logo is prominent on the black ribbed front, with the silver tuning scale and three knobs below. As the woman drifts out of view, the product remains alone against the blue tile, hanging steadily beneath the shower pipe. A dark blue title screen appears with the words “Splash Dance” in large, white, brush-style script, matching the logo on the product. The product is then shown in close detail. The black front fills most of the view, with the “Splash Dance” logo at the upper left. Lower down, the radio display and controls are shown: a small “Pollenex” nameplate, the words “AM/FM shower radio,” a horizontal AM/FM tuning scale, and three black knobs on the white panel. The labels beneath the knobs read “VOLUME,” “BAND,” and “TUNING,” with small markings such as “OFF” and “MAX” near the volume control and “FM” and “AM” near the band control. A side-by-side demonstration shows two ways the radio can be placed in a shower. On the left, the unit is mounted flat on the blue tiled wall, with bold white text below it reading “Affixes to wall.” On the right, another unit hangs from the shower pipe by straps near the spraying showerhead, with white text beside it reading “Clips to pipe.” The split view makes both installation positions visible at once. Back in the shower, the young woman appears beside the hanging radio again. Her wet hand passes in front of the black grille and logo, then she moves away from the unit, smiling and gesturing with her fingers near her face. Water beads on her skin and on the radio’s front. She looks toward the viewer and opens her mouth as if singing along, her expression bright and animated. Her wet hair swings slightly behind her as she faces forward, smiling with an open-mouthed, enthusiastic expression. A young adult man is then shown in the same kind of blue-tiled shower. He has short dark wet hair and bare shoulders. The white showerhead sprays diagonally behind him, and the Splash Dance radio hangs on the wall to his right. He rubs his hands together as if washing, holding or working with a white bar of soap. He points upward toward the showerhead and then toward the radio, glancing between the product and the viewer. His expression shifts from focused to playful. He lowers his hands, then breaks into an exaggerated cheerful pose, raising both arms with bent elbows as if dancing in the shower, mouth open in a big grin. The radio remains visible to his side, hanging near the spray. The radio is shown mounted directly on the tiled wall while a hand turns the right-hand tuning knob. The fingers grip the black knob and rotate it; then the hand drops away, leaving the unit centered on the blue tile. The “Splash Dance” logo, tuning scale, and three knobs remain visible. The setting changes to a bathtub: an adult blonde woman reclines in a white tub filled with water, bare shoulders above the surface. Her short, wet blonde hair is swept back. She rests both arms along the tub edges, eyes relaxed, with a calm smile. The Splash Dance radio is fixed on the tiled wall above and behind her, within easy reach but away from the waterline. She looks comfortable and still, appearing to enjoy the bath while the product sits prominently in the background. The earlier showering woman reappears in close view, wet hair slicked back, one hand near her ear and cheek. The hanging radio is beside her again, its black front wet with droplets. She tilts her head back slightly, then moves forward and to the side, leaving the radio more fully visible. The product hangs steady from its straps against the blue tiles, with the white controls below the black grille. Finally, a bold graphic fills the screen: a large pale-yellow ring or letter-like curve against a dark blue background, cropped so only part of the shape is visible.

Inside a bright train carriage, rows of passengers sit on both sides of a narrow center aisle. Sunlight pours through large windows, casting long shadows across the floor and seats. Many of the passengers are adult men dressed alike in crisp white dress shirts and dark ties, reading newspapers or folded papers in a quiet commuter-like atmosphere. A woman in a dark uniform stands in the aisle with her back turned, while passengers on either side sit upright, absorbed in reading. A young adult man in a white shirt and red tie sits by the window with a portable computer or briefcase-like device open in front of him. He holds a corded telephone handset to his ear, the coiled cord hanging down toward the device. Around him, other passengers crowd the seats; a blond woman leans back nearby, and other men in white shirts read or look down at papers. The train windows show blurred trees and countryside outside. Two men in white shirts and ties sit side by side reading newspapers. Both wear large eyeglasses; one is younger with dark hair, the other older with a receding hairline and a composed, serious expression. Behind them, another passenger’s newspaper rises over the seat back, hiding most of their face. A bright projectile streaks across the blue, and a glowing burst blooms overhead. The explosion transforms into a soft, colorful cloud of purples and pinks, opening like ink in water. Inside that expanding cloud, translucent Windows 11 interface panels appear. A large floating widget board materializes above the dunes, showing “11:11 AM” at the top, a search bar, a weather card reading “55°,” and other cards such as calendar and to-do lists. She drops downward into a grand, old-fashioned library or reading hall. Overhead is a large mural-like image with dramatic figures and a bright central glow. The woman falls or floats down through the high atrium, her red top billowing around her like a cape, and lands lightly near a white pedestal. A tiny green hummingbird darts over the surface and flies away from the pedestal, leading the view toward a huge arched opening in the library wall. Through the arch is a peaceful lake landscape with green trees, misty blue mountains, and still water reflecting the scenery. The woman now stands behind a large translucent panel in front of her, still inside the library space but visually connected to the outdoor lake scene. The hummingbird hovers near the panel. Outside, a person sits in a small canoe on the reflective lake beside the tall transparent chat window, making the digital messages feel physically present in the natural landscape. The imagery shifts underwater, with rippling blue light and shadowy movement, then returns to the woman in a dark blue, abstract space with the Windows 11 blue swirl pattern behind her. The commercial returns to the laptop on the small table in the dim room. On its screen, the dancer is visible in the studio, and the Windows 11 taskbar is centered along the bottom. A windowed video or communication interface opens beside the dance video, showing a smiling man in an outdoor setting at the top and a row of colorful thumbnails or tiles below. The woman’s hand rests near the keyboard as she looks at the screen, now back in her home environment, using the laptop to continue the connection that the earlier fantasy sequences visualized.

A hand with bright pink fingernails pushes a glossy red cartridge into the chrome stereo of an old car. A handwritten label on the cartridge reads “Born to be Wild.” The dashboard is vintage, with shiny metal knobs and a black-and-silver faceplate. The same hand then turns one of the round radio knobs. A small green tree-shaped air freshener hangs from the dashboard area. In the back seat, an older woman with short gray hair, hoop earrings, and a blue track-style jacket gestures animatedly with both hands while holding a melting ice pop. Beside her, another older woman with short white hair, black-framed glasses, orange earrings, layered necklaces, and a striped wrap continues knitting with the orange yarn. The group appears lively and chatty as the car continues along the coast. Another convertible appears ahead on the road, a light-colored classic car driven by an older man with silver hair and aviator sunglasses. He smiles broadly from behind the wheel with the ocean behind him. The women in the first car look toward him; the front passenger blows a kiss while still holding her teacup, the driver makes a surprised “ooh” expression with her hand near her cheek, the knitter reacts with her mouth open, and the woman in blue smiles while holding her ice pop. The driver then leans and grips the steering wheel as the car seems to jolt or swerve. A quick view near the roadside shows the dark convertible’s rear wheel passing over loose gravel beside a curb. The front passenger laughs with one arm raised high, and the women behind her react with delight as the car continues moving. The product is shown clearly inside a vehicle: a black WeatherTech floor mat with raised channels and a textured surface sits over dark carpet. The embossed “WeatherTech” name is visible along the lower edge. A turquoise teacup tips over onto the mat, spilling brown tea, a tea bag, and bits of soggy debris. In another view, pieces of a messy dessert or ice pop, with red filling and cream-colored fragments, fall onto the same style of mat. Back in the convertible, the white-haired driver in leopard print smiles and speaks while the others look toward her. The pink-shirted passenger relaxes beside her, and the knitter sits behind, watching. The driver’s expression shifts from pleased to determined, as if reassuring the group. The older man in the light convertible smiles again from his car, parked or moving slowly near the coast. The final view follows the dark convertible from behind as it drives along a sweeping coastal road. The ocean is bright blue on the right, rocky shoreline below, and steep cliffs rise on the left. One passenger raises both arms into the air in celebration while the car heads into the curve. The vehicle becomes smaller against the wide seaside landscape. Large on-screen text appears over the coastal road: “WeatherTech.com,” with “Tech” in red and the rest in black. It then changes to “WT.com” in large black letters. Beneath it is the WeatherTech logo, again with “Tech” in red, and a small line of text reading, “Auto. Home. Pet. Find Your Fit.”

A warmly lit home is decorated for the holidays. He wears a thick brown sweater and looks focused at the screen. A smiling adult man sits at a table with a silver Microsoft laptop in front of him. He has short dark hair and wears a dark sweatshirt. Food ingredients and a navy cap sit on the table in front of him, suggesting a casual home activity. The view moves to a Windows desktop interface. Along the bottom taskbar are familiar app icons, including the multicolored Copilot icon. A small rounded Copilot control panel opens above the taskbar. It contains several icons: the Copilot logo, a glasses-like symbol, a glowing microphone symbol in the center, a gear for settings, and an X to close. Then the laptop screen is shown from his side of the table. On screen is a dark smart-lighting control page, with sliders on the left, a large color wheel, rows of colored swatches, and control sections on the right. A small Copilot-style floating control bar sits near the bottom of the screen, and tiny text at the bottom reads “Screen simulated.” His hands rest near the keyboard and trackpad as the color selection changes on the interface, shifting from a blue-green tone to a bright red-pink. In the room behind the laptop, colorful holiday lights glow around the windows, visually matching the idea of syncing or adjusting lights. The man is then seen again from the front, still seated at the decorated table, with the windows behind him now glowing in red and green colors. The setting changes to a richly decorated workshop-like room filled with shelves of toys, boxes, clocks, and holiday objects. At the center, an older man with very long white hair and a full white beard, wearing a red top and suspenders, sits at a large desk with a silver Microsoft laptop. His appearance strongly resembles Santa Claus. Other people in festive clothing work in the background, including someone in green and red facing shelves on the right and an older woman at the left. The desk is crowded with old-fashioned objects, tools, papers, and shiny decorative items. The bearded man looks down at the laptop with a serious, slightly concerned expression. His laptop screen shows a presentation-style document with red accents. Large visible text reads “WORKSHOP QUARTERLY STATUS REPORT.” The page includes photos of groups of people or activity scenes, colored bullet points, and a slide navigation column on the left. His hand moves near the trackpad, and a small Copilot control bar remains visible near the bottom of the screen, again with “Screen simulated” shown in tiny text. After this, the older bearded man is seen again at the desk, still focused on the laptop. The older woman in the red patterned jacket and white turtleneck turns toward him from the side of the room, looking over with a curious, questioning expression. Her gray curly hair frames her face, and a globe and warm holiday lights sit behind her. The woman with glasses returns, seated at her laptop in the living room. She leans toward the screen with a thoughtful, slightly intent expression. Behind her, holiday decorating continues, and the golden dog remains on the floor at the right. The scene then shifts back to the smiling man from earlier, now clearly in a kitchen or dining area. He wears a plaid holiday apron over his dark shirt and stands behind the laptop with bowls, measuring cups, tomatoes, and other cooking ingredients spread across the counter. He holds two tomatoes in one hand while looking toward the computer, as if asking for help with a recipe. In the background, a person sits at a table, and a decorated Christmas tree and string lights add to the festive setting. The moustached man in the brown sweater appears again at his dining table, now looking more concerned or puzzled as he faces the laptop. On his screen, two windows are open side by side. On the left is an image or video window showing a large inflatable reindeer in a front yard at night, standing near a house decorated with lights. On the right is a document with the bold title “HOA GUIDELINES.” The document is laid out like a formal rules page with paragraphs beneath the title. The man’s hands rest near the keyboard and trackpad, and the Copilot control bar sits along the bottom edge of the screen. Through the windows behind the laptop, colored holiday lights glow outside and around the room. The man is then seen from behind, seated alone at the long table, facing a wall of windows framed by garlands and strings of lights. The room is filled with warm holiday color: red and green reflections, small lit decorations, and a Christmas tree or illuminated display near the right side. White on-screen text appears across the center: “Ready for the holidays?” A moment later the text changes to: “Meet the computer you can talk to.” The final image is a soft, bright pastel background with subtle sparkles and the Copilot logo beside the words “Copilot on Windows 11.”

A college campus appears in warm autumn colours. Red leaves fill the upper left, and golden foliage surrounds a stone archway. Beneath the arch, students move through a shadowy entrance. A young woman with shoulder-length red hair, wearing a light patterned sweater and jeans, walks beside a stocky blond young man in a red varsity jacket with gold sleeves and a large letter on the chest. Both carry books or folders, suggesting they are students. As they stroll and talk, the woman gestures with papers in her arms. A yellow folder slips or falls to the ground near their feet. The young man notices, bends down, and picks it up while still holding several books against his side. He straightens, smiling and continuing the conversation with her. The scene shifts to a long, arched stone corridor with bright windows along the left and a row of bicycles parked on the right. In the left foreground, a student struggles under a bulky rolled-up white object, possibly bedding or a rug, draped over his shoulders, with bags or fabric hanging around him. He shuffles along awkwardly near the windows, partly blocking another student in red clothing. The corridor feels like an old campus building, with repeating arches stretching into the distance and scattered leaves on the floor.
